transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-22
Start: 14:30 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Lena Ortiz (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Stratify Head of ML), Tom Alvarez (Sr SWE), Priya Nair (Infra)

Summary (auto): quick technical deep dive covering vector dimensionality trade-offs, batching strategies, KV cache behavior for rerank pipelines, quantized model footprints, and on-prem/VPC constraints for the pilot. Agreed: Redwood to deliver bench scenarios and cost deltas; customer to provide sample queries and SLOs; target pilot kickoff early April.

[00:00] Lena Ortiz: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Quick agenda — we want to focus on the rerank path: how vector dims affect latency and throughput, ideal batch sizes, when KV-cache helps vs when it doesn't, and what the on‑prem pilot pre‑reqs look like. Any additions?
[00:17] Maya Chen: No, that covers it. We especially need clarity on 95th pctl latency impact when we move from 512 to 1024 dims — that's our main concern for user-facing search.
[00:27] Ravi Patel: Great, I'll share some numbers and heuristics, and later we'll sketch the pilot infra constraints. Also flagging quantized model options — 8bit vs 4bit — because that changes memory and throughput.
[00:40] Tom Alvarez: Quick note: our current production vectors are 768 dim from an in-house model. We have about 200 qps typical, peaking 700 qps; tail latency SLO is 150 ms for top-k rerank (not including client network).
[00:55] Priya Nair: On infra side, we need the VPC connectivity, KMS details, and ideally no public internet egress for the model runtime during pilot.

[01:12] Ravi Patel: Understood. Start with vector dims: rule of thumb we use — doubling dims roughly increases per-vector compute ~linearly for the dot-product stage and increases memory, but the runtime kernel shape matters. For 512 vs 1024 we typically see ~1.6x to 2.1x latency increase depending on CPU/GPU kernels and whether we're using fused GEMM kernels. For quantized int8 paths, the perf hit is lower because bandwidth improvements compensate.
[01:45] Maya Chen: When you say "latency increase", is that per-token or end-to-end rerank? We need end-to-end numbers including embedding + kNN + rerank scoring.
[01:55] Ravi Patel: Good point. My ballpark was for the embed vector generation and scoring kernel. For end-to-end you add nearest neighbor search time which scales with index size and dimension — approximate: ANN search increases with dimension because distance ops cost more and index sizes grow. For small candidate sets (top 100) the dominant cost is scoring.
[02:20] Lena Ortiz: I'll interject: in Redwood's hybrid flow customers often do an ANN retrieval to pull ~200 candidates then rerank with cross-encoder or MLP on embeddings to produce final top 5. If your candidate set is small, scoring latency dominates; if it's large, ANN search can dominate.

[02:40] Tom Alvarez: Our current pipeline: embed(query) -> FAISS ANN with IVF-PQ -> get 200 -> rerank MLP (512 dims) -> return top 5. We're concerned switching to 1024 because memory and inference time will spike.
[02:55] Ravi Patel: Right. A few levers: batch size on embed generation can help amortize overhead when you have bursts, but for single query interactive SLO you want small batch (1-8). For throughput-oriented backfills, batches of 32-128 make sense. Also KV-cache helps when you have repeated prefixes or repeated queries per session — but for stateless query rerank it's less helpful unless you cache query embeddings or cached top-k results.
[03:25] Maya Chen: We do a lot of slightly-rephrased queries — similar but not identical. Does KV-cache help at the embedding level?
[03:31] Ravi Patel: KV-cache is most effective for autoregressive decoders where past key/value states are reused across incremental tokens. For embedding-only workloads, you get more mileage from embedding caching (i.e., store query -> vector hash). If many queries are near-duplicates, a lightweight similarity cache helps. We can also cache ANN results for hot queries.
[03:55] Priya Nair: For on‑prem, what is footprint difference? If we go from 512 to 1024 and use int8 quant, what's memory on GPU we should expect?
[04:03] Ravi Patel: Example numbers: unquantized FP16 512-d model ~2-3 GB GPU memory (model only, depends on architecture). 1024-d FP16 could be ~4.5-6 GB. With int8 quantization you often cut model memory by ~2x, so 1024 int8 might be 2.5-3 GB. These are rough; exact depends on tokenizer, KV cache sizes, and extra runtime overhead. We'll run explicit measured benches and give a table.
[04:35] Tom Alvarez: Ok that's helpful. Can you share a cost delta? We're comparing hosted vs dedicated vs on‑prem.
[04:42] Lena Ortiz: We will — Ravi will produce cost-per-1M-token or cost-per-embedding scenarios with various dims and batch sizes. For embeddings the unit is usually per-embedding compute rather than per-token. For dedicated we model reserved GPU hours; on‑prem cost is mostly infra amortization and ops.

[04:58] Ravi Patel: A second dimension is batching tradeoffs: at low-latency SLOs (<=150 ms p95) batching beyond 16 often harms p95 despite improving throughput. For GPU runtimes we tune batch pipelines: small batches + fewer concurrent streams for low tail vs larger batches for throughput. We recommend dynamic batching configuration: target 8 for interactive, 64 for bulk.
[05:28] Maya Chen: Our worst case is a 10% user base with complex queries that hit p95. We need sustainable p95 regardless of burst. Can Redwood do autoscaling on‑prem to protect p95?
[05:38] Ravi Patel: Autoscaling on‑prem is trickier but doable: we support an on‑prem agent that can spin up containers across a cluster, but it's constrained by your hardware pool. For true autoscaling like cloud-level we'd pair dedicated mode. For pilot we can show scaling policies and a fallback model that is smaller / quantized to keep latency bounded.
[05:58] Priya Nair: Fallback models — you mean model variants in the catalog?
[06:02] Lena Ortiz: Exactly. Canary/fallback: if your primary 1024-d model exceeds latency thresholds, traffic can be routed to a 512-d quantized model with lower compute. That gives graceful degradation.

[06:20] Tom Alvarez: About batch shaping — do you implement dynamic batching based on observed queue depth?
[06:25] Ravi Patel: Yes, our runtime has continuous batching and a queue-aware batching policy. It will wait up to X ms to form a batch or flush early to meet SLO. You can configure the max wait time and max batch size. For interactive SLOs we keep max wait small (3-7 ms) and cap batch to 8-16. For throughput we raise those.
[06:45] Maya Chen: What about network effects inside VPC — if model runtime is in a private subnet, do you see any added serialization cost?
[06:52] Ravi Patel: Network cost is mainly RPC overhead; in a colocated VPC the RPCs are sub-ms. If you separate the retrieval service and model runtime across different hosts, you add hop costs. We recommend colocating retrieval and rerank runtime in the same subnet for low-latency critical path.
[07:10] Priya Nair: For the pilot we'll need KMS integration and we prefer HSM for keys. Is Redwood compatible?
[07:15] Lena Ortiz: Yes, we support customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations; we'll send the security checklist.

[07:25] [Speaker 1 - automatic]: umm sorry background noise, I think Tom had a question about embedding caching semantics —
[07:31] Tom Alvarez: Yeah, just clarifying — if we cache embeddings at an LRU layer, what's eviction and consistency implications if model changes? We retrain models quarterly.
[07:40] Ravi Patel: Good question. Cache invalidation policy depends on your model update cadence. We recommend versioned cache keys: model-id + vector-hash. When you deploy a new model, the cache misses until warmed. For gradual rollouts you can keep old and new caches in parallel keyed by model version.
[08:00] Maya Chen: On the subject of quantization — we saw quality drop for our reranker at 4-bit. What's Redwood's guidance?
[08:07] Ravi Patel: 8-bit is typically safe for embedding generation; 4-bit can introduce quality variance, especially for fine-grained ranking. For rerank where small score differences matter, start with 8-bit and run evals on your prompt sets. Redwood Optimize can run automated jitter tests against your gold set and flag regressions.
[08:30] Lena Ortiz: We'll include an eval plan in the bench deliverable: precision@k comparisons across dims/quantization combos.

[08:40] Maya Chen: Does Redwood provide tooling to replay queries for p95 testing?
[08:44] Ravi Patel: Yes, we have a replay harness that can replay your representative queries at target QPS and measure p50/p95/p99 and tail behaviors. That's part of the pilot engagement.
[08:55] Priya Nair: For on‑prem deployment we have stricter egress — logs must go to our SIEM via private channel. Does Redwood support that?
[09:02] Lena Ortiz: Yes, we can configure log sinks to your SIEM over private endpoints and you can opt for local log retention only. We'll include details in the security checklist.

[09:15] Tom Alvarez: Back to cost: can you give a quick hypothetical? Say 1M queries per month, average vector dim 768, median batch 8, 200 qps baseline — how would hosted vs on‑prem look?
[09:29] Ravi Patel: Rough quickback: hosted API may be $X per 1M embeddings (we'll give exact table) — dedicated reserved GPU hours reduces per-embedding cost by ~30-50% depending on utilization. On‑prem cost depends on hardware amortization; with good utilization you'd be competitive with dedicated. The missing piece for you is ops overhead — if you have SREs to manage, on‑prem becomes more attractive. We'll send concrete numbers.

[09:55] Maya Chen: Okay sounds great. Anything else on batching or KV-cache?
[10:00] Ravi Patel: One last note: for rerank scoring kernels we recently added fused-vector-matmul for 512/768 shapes which reduces latency significantly; performance cliff happens when dims misalign with kernel tiling — so pick dims that map well to vendor kernels when possible (multiples of 32/64 depending on hardware). We'll include kernel alignment notes per GPU type.
[10:25] Priya Nair: That's very practical. We'll check our internal tooling to see if 768 is kernel-friendly on our GPUs.

[10:35] Lena Ortiz: Recap/next steps: Ravi to run bench matrix (dims: 512/768/1024; quant: FP16/8bit/4bit; batch sizes 1/8/32/64) and share CSV + cost deltas by 03/25. Maya to share 1k sample queries + target SLOs by 03/27. We'll schedule pilot kickoff week of 04/06. Any objections?
[10:58] Maya Chen: None. Thanks everyone.
[11:02] Tom Alvarez: Thanks, good call.
[11:05] Priya Nair: Thanks, bye.

End transcript.
